title: Distance & Slope
description: Measure how far apart points are and how steep a line is, with the common pitfalls

blocks.text: Two of the most basic geometric measurements are the distance between two points and the slope of the line through them. They sound simple, but each has a pitfall that trips up beginners.
We will cover the formulas and, just as importantly, how to avoid the floating point and edge case traps that come with them.
The distance between two points comes straight from the Pythagorean theorem. The horizontal gap and vertical gap are the two legs of a right triangle, and the distance is the hypotenuse.

blocks.caption: Distance is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs dx and dy

blocks.text: So the distance equals the square root of dx squared plus dy squared, where dx and dy are the coordinate differences.
The square root is slow and introduces floating point error. A key trick: when you only need to compare distances, or check against a threshold, compare the squared distances instead.
Since squaring preserves order for non negative values, the closer point has the smaller squared distance too. This keeps everything in exact integer arithmetic.

Rule of thumb:

Only take the square root when you truly need the actual distance value. For comparisons, sorting, or radius checks, squared distance is faster and exact.
The slope measures steepness: how much the line rises for each step it runs sideways. It is the change in y divided by the change in x, often said as rise over run.

blocks.caption: Slope is rise over run, and is undefined for a vertical line

blocks.text: A positive slope climbs left to right, a negative slope falls, and a slope of zero is a flat horizontal line.
Slope has a dangerous edge case. A vertical line has zero run, so the slope divides by zero and is undefined. Code that computes slope directly will crash or produce infinity here.
Comparing slopes as fractions also risks floating point error, so two points that are really collinear might look slightly off. For these reasons, slope is often the wrong tool for exact geometry.

content.title: 5. Better Collinearity with the Cross Product

blocks.text: To check whether three points lie on one line, do not compare slopes. Instead use the cross product. Three points are collinear exactly when the cross product of the two vectors from the first point is zero.
This avoids division entirely, handles vertical lines with no special case, and stays exact with integer coordinates. It is the professional way to test collinearity.

codes.python:
def collinear(a, b, c):
    return (b[0]-a[0]) * (c[1]-a[1]) - (b[1]-a[1]) * (c[0]-a[0]) == 0   # cross product is zero

content.title: 6. Where Distance and Slope Show Up

blocks.text: These measurements anchor many geometry tasks.

items: Finding the closest or farthest pair of points, using squared distance
Grouping points that lie on the same line
Radius and range checks around a point
Detecting collinear triples, best done with the cross product

blocks.text: Prefer squared distance and the cross product over raw distance and slope whenever you can, for both speed and correctness.
